name: โรคไตอักเสบ
preview_text: ใน TCM โรคไตอักเสบไม่ได้เป็นเพียงปัญหาเกี่ยวกับไตเท่านั้น แต่ยังสะท้อนถึงความไม่สมดุลทางรัฐธรรมนูญอย่างลึกซึ้ง และการรักษารูปแบบที่ซ่อนอยู่สามารถลดภาวะโปรตีนในปัสสาวะ และทำให้เด็กมีเสถียรภาพ...
synonyms: ["Nephritic Syndrome", "Inflammation Of The Kidneys", "Kidney Inflammation", "Acute Nephritis", "Acute Kidney Disease", "Sudden Onset Of Nephritis"]
conventional_description: Nephritis refers to inflammation of the kidneys, most commonly caused by autoimmune disorders (like IgA nephropathy or lupus nephritis), infections, or reactions to medications. The inflammation damages the glomeruli - the tiny filtering units that clean the blood - leading to protein and sometimes blood leaking into the urine. Typical symptoms include foamy urine (from protein), cola-colored or visibly bloody urine, swelling around the eyes, hands, or feet, and high blood pressure. Diagnosis is usually made through urine tests, blood work (kidney function and antibody panels), imaging, and sometimes a kidney biopsy.
conventional_treatments: Conventional treatment aims to reduce inflammation and slow kidney damage. Mild cases may be managed with blood pressure medications (especially ACE inhibitors or ARBs) that also reduce protein leakage. More active inflammation often requires corticosteroids and other immunosuppressants like cyclophosphamide or mycophenolate. Diuretics help control edema, and dietary changes - particularly limiting salt, potassium, and protein - are standard. In advanced disease, dialysis or kidney transplant may become necessary.
tcm_understanding:
TCM understands nephritis primarily through the lens of the Kidney and Spleen organ systems. The Kidneys govern water metabolism and store the body's most precious essence (Jing). When Kidney Qi and Yin are depleted, the kidneys lose their ability to hold onto essence, so vital proteins leak into the urine - a phenomenon TCM calls "essence not being secured." The Spleen, meanwhile, transforms and transports fluids; when its Yang is weak, dampness accumulates and spills into the tissues, causing the edema so common in nephritis.
But deficiency is only half the story. When Dampness lingers too long, it can combine with Heat to create Damp-Heat in the Lower Burner - a hot, turbid condition that directly inflames the kidneys and bladder, producing cloudy, burning urine and accelerating the damage. In chronic cases, the sluggish flow caused by both deficiency and dampness leads to Blood Stagnation, where the tiny vessels inside the kidneys become congested and scarred, locking in a cycle of persistent proteinuria and hematuria.
This is why one Western diagnosis can have multiple TCM causes: a young person with an acute post-infectious nephritis might present with pure Damp-Heat, while an older patient with a long history of autoimmune nephritis might show Qi and Yin Deficiency with superimposed Blood Stasis. The tongue and pulse tell the practitioner which pattern is active, and treatment shifts accordingly - cooling and draining in acute phases, nourishing and invigorating in chronic ones.
classical_quote: 「诸湿肿满，皆属于脾...其本在肾，其末在肺。」
classical_translation: "All dampness, swelling, and fullness are attributed to the Spleen... The root lies in the Kidneys, the branch in the Lungs."

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner first looks at the overall energy landscape. Nephritis often involves both a weakened foundation and a build‑up of unwelcome factors. The most common root is Qi and Yin Deficiency, where the body lacks both vital Qi and cooling Yin. Someone with this pattern appears tired and pale, yet the tongue is red with little coating and the pulse feels thin and rapid - signs that point to deep depletion rather than a simple energy slump.
If the person complains of feeling cold, with noticeable puffiness around the eyes or ankles, the focus shifts to Kidney and Spleen Yang Deficiency. Here the warming, transforming power of Yang is low, so fluid accumulates. The tongue is pale and swollen, often with teeth marks, and the pulse is deep and slow. A practitioner will ask about cold hands and feet, loose stools, and a heavy sensation in the low back - all clues that the fire of the Kidneys and Spleen needs stoking.
When the urine is cloudy, dark, or contains visible blood, Damp-Heat in the Lower Burner is a prime suspect. This pattern brings a sense of internal mugginess and heat: a bitter taste in the mouth, a heavy or burning sensation during urination, and a tongue that is red with a thick, greasy yellow coat. The pulse feels slippery and fast, like a stream rushing after a storm. The practitioner checks whether the symptoms flare after rich or spicy foods, which can feed Damp-Heat.
In longstanding nephritis, the practitioner also searches for Blood Stagnation. Persistent proteinuria that does not improve with tonics, a dark or purplish tongue with stasis spots, and a choppy pulse all suggest that the micro‑circulation of the Kidneys is obstructed. Fixed, stabbing pain in the low back is another telltale sign. This pattern rarely stands alone - it often lurks behind a deficiency pattern, making the illness stubborn and slow to resolve.

patterns.symptoms: ["Fatigue that worsens with exertion", "Dry mouth and throat, especially at night", "Warm sensation in palms, soles, and chest", "Scanty, dark urine", "Red tongue with little or no coating", "Thready, rapid pulse"]
patterns.worse_with: Emotional stress, worry, or overthinking, Spicy, greasy, or fried foods, Overwork and insufficient sleep
patterns.better_with: Adequate rest and sleep, Cool, moistening foods (pears, lily bulb), Gentle movement or exercise
patterns.why_this_happens: The kidneys govern water and store essence. When Qi and Yin are both depleted, the kidney's ability to manage fluids and retain essence weakens, so protein (essence) leaks into the urine and mild edema can appear. Qi deficiency causes the deep fatigue and breathlessness, while Yin deficiency creates a background of dry mouth, warm palms, and dark, scanty urine.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with little or no coating, possibly cracked and dry. Pulse: thready (fine) and weak, often rapid.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Qi and Yin are already depleted, so rest and nourishing foods directly replenish them. Overwork and emotional strain consume Qi and stir up heat, further damaging Yin. Spicy and drying foods create internal heat that deepens the Yin deficiency, while gentle movement supports Qi circulation without depleting it.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Prioritize rest and avoid overwork. Eat nourishing, moist foods like pears, lily bulbs, and millet congee; steer clear of spicy, fried, or drying foods that consume Yin. Gentle daily movement such as walking or Tai Chi helps Qi flow without exhausting it.

patterns.worse_with: Cold, raw foods and iced drinks, Prolonged standing or overwork, Damp, cold environments, Emotional stress, worry, or overthinking
patterns.better_with: Warmth on the lower back, Eating warm, cooked meals, Gentle movement or exercise, Adequate rest and sleep
patterns.why_this_happens: In nephritis, Kidney and Spleen Yang Deficiency weakens the body's ability to transform and transport fluids. The Spleen fails to manage water, leading to dampness accumulation and edema, while the Kidney fails to warm and consolidate, causing cold limbs and loss of essential proteins in the urine. This dual deficiency creates a cycle of cold, water retention, and fatigue.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, swollen, puffy body with teeth marks and a white slippery coating. Pulse: deep, weak, slow; both Chi positions are especially feeble.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Kidney and Spleen Yang are like the body's pilot light-they warm and transform. Cold foods and damp environments extinguish that fire, worsening water retention and fatigue. Warmth, cooked foods, and rest preserve Yang and help the body move fluids, which is why symptoms improve with these habits.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked foods like soups, stews, and congees. Avoid cold, raw, and iced items. Keep the lower back and feet warm, and get gentle daily movement to support circulation.

patterns.worse_with: Spicy, greasy, or fried foods, Alcohol, Humid weather, Prolonged sitting or inactivity
patterns.better_with: Light, bland diet, Drinking plenty of water, Cool, dry weather, Gentle movement or exercise
patterns.why_this_happens: In TCM, the kidneys and bladder belong to the Lower Burner. When Dampness and Heat accumulate there, they disrupt the kidney's ability to separate clear fluids from turbid waste. The Heat scorches the blood vessels, causing blood to leak into the urine, while the Dampness makes the urine cloudy and heavy. This internal stew of Heat and Dampness also irritates the urinary passages, leading to burning and urgency, and can cause edema when fluids overflow into tissues.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: Red body, slightly swollen, with a yellow greasy coating thickest at the root. Pulse: Slippery (Hua) and rapid (Shu), more pronounced at the rear position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Greasy, spicy foods and alcohol create more Dampness and Heat in the body, directly feeding the pattern. Humid weather adds external Dampness, while sitting still allows Dampness to sink and stagnate. A light diet and hydration help flush out the Lower Burner, and gentle movement promotes the circulation of Qi to transform Dampness.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid heavy, greasy, and spicy foods that feed Dampness and Heat. Cut out alcohol and sugary drinks. Drink plenty of plain water and eat more cooling, diuretic foods like cucumber, watermelon, and mung beans. Gentle daily movement like walking helps move stagnant Dampness.

patterns.why_this_happens: When nephritis becomes chronic, the ongoing inflammation and sluggish Qi flow cause blood to congeal in the tiny vessels of the kidneys. This stasis damages the kidney's delicate filtering network, so protein and red blood cells persistently leak into the urine. The fixed, stabbing pain in the lower back is a direct signal that blood is stuck and obstructing the collaterals.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: dark purple body, stasis spots, distended sublingual veins, thin white coating. Pulse: choppy (涩 sè), rough and uneven.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Blood stasis is like a river that has frozen over; cold and stillness cause it to congeal further, while warmth and gentle movement encourage flow. Stress tightens the Liver Qi, which can worsen stagnation, so keeping calm and active is essential.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat moderate amounts of blood-moving foods like turmeric, hawthorn berries, and a little black fungus. Avoid cold, raw foods and icy drinks which congeal blood. Gentle daily movement such as walking or tai chi helps keep Qi and blood flowing.

faqs.question: Can TCM cure nephritis?
faqs.answer: TCM views nephritis as a condition that can be managed and often significantly improved, but "cure" depends on the underlying cause and how early treatment begins. In acute, post-infectious cases driven by Damp-Heat, complete resolution is possible with herbs that clear heat and drain dampness. In chronic autoimmune forms, the goal shifts to long-term stabilization: reducing proteinuria, protecting kidney function, and preventing relapses. Many patients are able to reduce their reliance on immunosuppressive drugs under their doctor's supervision while using TCM.

faqs.question: How long does it take to see results with Chinese medicine?
faqs.answer: Edema and urinary symptoms often improve within the first 2-4 weeks. Proteinuria reduction is a slower process - noticeable changes on lab tests typically take 2-3 months of consistent treatment. Deficiency patterns require patience; rebuilding Kidney Qi and Yin is like refilling a deep well, and it cannot be rushed. Most patients commit to a 3-6 month initial course, with periodic reassessment.

faqs.question: Can I take Chinese herbs alongside my blood pressure or immunosuppressive medications?
faqs.answer: Yes, in most cases TCM and Western medications can be used together safely, but this must be coordinated carefully. Never stop or adjust your prescribed medications on your own. Some herbs, particularly those that move blood (like Dan Shen or Tao Ren), can interact with anticoagulants. Diuretic herbs may amplify the effect of pharmaceutical diuretics. Always bring a complete list of your medications to your TCM practitioner, and inform your nephrologist that you are using Chinese medicine.

faqs.question: Is acupuncture safe for someone with kidney disease?
faqs.answer: Yes, acupuncture is generally very safe for kidney patients when performed by a licensed practitioner using sterile, single-use needles. The points used for nephritis are mostly on the lower back and legs and do not directly puncture the kidneys. However, if you are on blood thinners or have severely impaired kidney function, inform your acupuncturist, as bleeding risk may be higher and point selection may be adjusted.

faqs.question: What foods should I avoid if I have nephritis?
faqs.answer: From a TCM perspective, cold, raw foods and iced drinks weaken the Spleen Yang and promote dampness, so they should be minimized. Greasy, fried, and spicy foods create Damp-Heat and can aggravate inflammation. Excess salt burdens the kidneys and worsens edema, so a low-sodium diet is important. Dairy and sugar also tend to generate dampness and phlegm, so they should be used sparingly. Your practitioner will give you more specific guidance based on your pattern.

faqs.question: Will I need to keep taking herbs forever?
faqs.answer: Typically not. Once kidney function stabilizes and proteinuria is reduced to a safe level, many patients transition to a maintenance phase - a lower dose of herbs, or taking them only during high-risk periods (like cold and flu season) to prevent flares. Some choose to continue with gentle, food-grade herbs or periodic acupuncture for long-term resilience. The goal is always to reach a point where the body can maintain balance with minimal intervention.

faqs.question: Can TCM help with the side effects of steroids?
faqs.answer: Yes, this is an area where TCM excels. Long-term corticosteroid use often creates a pattern of Yin Deficiency with Damp-Heat - symptoms like night sweats, irritability, moon face, and fluid retention. Herbal formulas that nourish Yin and gently drain dampness can mitigate these side effects, making the medication more tolerable. As the steroid dose is gradually tapered under medical supervision, herbs can support the adrenal glands and reduce the risk of relapse.

research.title: Chinese herbal medicine for chronic glomerulonephritis: a systematic review and meta-analysis
research.description: A meta-analysis of 22 RCTs involving over 2,000 patients found that adding Chinese herbal medicine to conventional therapy significantly reduced 24-hour proteinuria and improved serum creatinine compared to conventional therapy alone. Common patterns treated included Qi and Yin Deficiency and Spleen-Kidney Yang Deficiency.
research.periodical: Zhang L, et al. Chinese Journal of Integrative Medicine, 2019.

research.title: Clinical observation on Shen Qi Di Huang Tang for chronic nephritis with Qi and Yin Deficiency
research.description: A clinical trial with 120 patients showed that Shen Qi Di Huang Tang combined with Western medicine reduced urinary protein and improved fatigue scores more than Western medicine alone. Tongue and pulse improvements were also noted.
research.periodical: Wang Y, et al. Journal of Traditional Chinese Medicine, 2020.

research.title: Acupuncture for chronic kidney disease-related symptoms: a pilot randomized controlled trial
research.description: A small pilot RCT of 60 patients with chronic kidney disease, including nephritis, found that acupuncture on Shenshu (BL-23), Taixi (KI-3), and Zusanli (ST-36) significantly reduced back pain and fatigue compared to sham acupuncture, with no adverse events.
research.periodical: Li X, et al. Evidence-Based Complementary and Alternative Medicine, 2021.
